lessons.title: Give new information a familiar home
lessons.anchor: Start with something you already know.
lessons.prerequisites: None.

pages.title: A small experiment
pages.html:
We will use connections to make new information easier to remember. First, try a short recall task. There is nothing to study yet.

On the next page, press Play when you are ready. A number will appear for ten seconds and then disappear. Try to remember it without copying it.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source number and date association are retained. No speed-of-learning claim is repeated. Interactive recall, replay and accessibility controls are adaptations.

pages.title: Ten seconds to remember
pages.prompt: When the number disappears, type what you remember. Leading zeroes matter.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source number and date association are retained. No speed-of-learning claim is repeated. Interactive recall, replay and accessibility controls are adaptations.

pages.title: Give the digits meaning
pages.html:
The source demonstration connects the number to two dates: 04 July 1776 and 11 September 2001.

07041776 · 09112001

The digits use month–day–year order: 07/04/1776 and 09/11/2001. If the events are familiar to you, they provide two anchors for an otherwise long string. If they are unfamiliar, the association will be less useful to you.

The point we will use throughout this course: connect new information to established old information.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source number and date association are retained. No speed-of-learning claim is repeated. Interactive recall, replay and accessibility controls are adaptations.

pages.title: What made a useful connection?
pages.prompt: Which explanation fits this demonstration?
options: A familiar meaning can help organise new information.
A meaningful connection guarantees perfect recall.
pages.explanation: The number stayed the same. A familiar association can provide a way to organise and retrieve it; your own recall may vary.

pages.title: Use the idea with letters
pages.html:
Next, we will connect Hebrew letter shapes to familiar images. Choose an association that helps you recognise the printed letter. Then try to recall it before looking at the explanation again.

For a personal practice round, think of three familiar objects. Look away, name them, do a different short task, and try once more.

pages.title: Three shapes, three sounds
pages.html:
מMem: /m/, as in mountain.

נNun: /n/, as in nose.

תTav: /t/, as in tripping.

Focus first on the printed shape and its sound. The letter names will become familiar through use.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Source mnemonics retained as text. Original mnemonic drawings/audio are not fabricated. Recognition replaces tracing, following Guy’s decision.

pages.title: Attach each shape to an image
pages.html:
Guy’s source mnemonics are mountain-climber for מ, nose for נ, and tripping for ת.

Look at one letter, say its sound, then look away and picture it. Use the association to recover the shape.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Source mnemonics retained as text. Original mnemonic drawings/audio are not fabricated. Recognition replaces tracing, following Guy’s decision.

pages.title: Two letters have an end form
pages.html:
מ → םMem at the end of a word uses ם.

נ → ןNun at the end of a word uses ן.

The final form changes the shape, not the identity of the letter. Tav keeps the same shape at the end.

pages.title: Find the beginning
pages.html:
Hebrew words run from right to left. In the printed sequence below, start with the rightmost letter.

מנת

The reading order is Mem, then Nun, then Tav. We are identifying letters here, not guessing the word’s vowels.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Only printed forms are required. Handwriting remains optional off-screen practice; no tracing or simulated script glyphs.

pages.title: Keep the right shape at the end
pages.html:
The end of a Hebrew word is on its left. A final Mem or Nun takes its final shape there.

תןTav, then final Nun: the leftmost letter ends the string.

תםTav, then final Mem.

These are letter-order exercises at this stage. Their meanings are not new vocabulary targets.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Only printed forms are required. Handwriting remains optional off-screen practice; no tracing or simulated script glyphs.

pages.title: Print and handwriting
pages.html:
The course uses printed, or block, letters. Hebrew also has handwritten forms, often called script. These can look different while representing the same letters.

For now, recognise and type the printed forms. Optional handwriting practice belongs in a separate printable resource.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Only printed forms are required. Handwriting remains optional off-screen practice; no tracing or simulated script glyphs.

pages.title: Letters and vowel marks
pages.html:
Compare the same Mem with three different marks. Read the letter and then its vowel.

מַma — the line supplies /a/.

מֶme — the dots supply /e/.

מִmi — the single dot supplies /i/.

The vowel marks are called Nikkud. We will use them to make unfamiliar readings explicit.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source’s blanket horizontal-line rule is narrowed to the displayed patah/qamats examples. Hataf-qamats is not taught as /a/. Source nonsense strings are identified as decoding practice. Silent sheva is introduced earlier for the revised route.

pages.title: Recognise the familiar patterns
pages.html:
The displayed מַ and מָ examples are read with /a/. Guy’s mnemonic is a horizontal line for the open “aaaa” sound.

מֶ and מֵ show /e/. The pair of dots is like elephant eyes. מִ has one itsy-bitsy dot for /i/.

Learn the reading of the supplied examples. These shortcuts do not mean every superficially similar mark always has the same sound.

pages.title: Three more letter shapes
pages.html:
אAlef: Guy’s source image is an albatross/eagle.

הHe: the source image connects its shape to a throat and the /h/ sound.

יYod: the small letter connects to “itsy-bitsy”.

pages.title: Letters can have different roles
pages.html:
In the supplied words, these letters sometimes represent a consonant and sometimes help write a vowel. Use the whole modelled word to decide their role.

יָםsea — the initial Yod has a /y/ sound.

מָתָנָהgift — the final He is not pronounced as /h/ here.

אִמָּאmother — follow the vowel reading supplied with Alef.

pages.title: Keep the whole word together

מַיִםwater

pages.title: Speaker, listener, someone else
pages.html:
A pronoun points to a person or group already clear in the conversation.

I is the speaker. You is the person being addressed. She and they refer to people being talked about, who may also be present.

אניI — used by a male or female speaker.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Human-written source retained in shortened form. He and we remain at their later readable stages. Social judgments about everyday variants are omitted.

pages.title: Four ways to address you
pages.html:
אתהyou — one man or boy

אתyou — one woman or girl

אתםyou — a male or mixed group

אתןyou — an all-female group

The shared opening את helps connect the four forms. Choose by who is being addressed.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Human-written source retained in shortened form. He and we remain at their later readable stages. Social judgments about everyday variants are omitted.

pages.title: Talk about someone
pages.html:
היאshe

הםthey — a male or mixed group

הןthey — an all-female group

These are subject pronouns. Object forms such as “me” and “her” come later. “He” and “we” also arrive after their remaining letters.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Human-written source retained in shortened form. He and we remain at their later readable stages. Social judgments about everyday variants are omitted.

pages.title: I am …
pages.html:
אני אמן.I am an artist — a male speaker in this example.

היא אמא.She is a mother.

English puts “am” or “is” between the two parts. These ordinary present-tense Hebrew sentences connect the person and the description without an added word for “am/is”.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source nominal-sentence explanation is adapted to the available words. Adjective agreement and attributive constructions remain later.

pages.title: Keep the two parts visible
pages.html:
In אתה אמן., אתה identifies the person. אמן tells us who that person is.

You already know the pronoun, so only the new noun meaning has to be learned. Change one part and read the new sentence again.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The source nominal-sentence explanation is adapted to the available words. Adjective agreement and attributive constructions remain later.

pages.title: A greeting and a description
pages.html:
היי, אני אמא.Hi, I am a mother.

היי is the supplied spelling of the greeting. Keep its doubled Yod as part of the word; the spelling return will make another connection later.

Use אמת for truth, אי for island, תה for tea and תאנה for fig in the vocabulary round.

pages.title: Meet ו
pages.html:
וֹA dot above accompanies the /o/ reading.

וּA dot in the letter accompanies the /u/ reading.

וAs a consonant, Vav represents /v/.

pages.title: Find it in words
pages.html:
הוּאhe — the Vav writes /u/ in this word.

אוֹor — the Vav writes /o/.

תּוּתstrawberry — /u/ again.

תָּוmusical note or mark — the final Vav is /v/.

pages.title: The gift
pages.html:
מתנהa gift / gift

המתנהthe gift

The prefix ה־ attaches to the noun. Hebrew has no separate word corresponding to English “a” or “an” in this example.

sourceRefs.adaptation: And is excerpted from the later source lesson; examples use the revised earlier vocabulary. Prefix vowels are word-specific models.

pages.title: From someone
pages.html:
המתנה מאמא.The gift is from Mom.

The מ־ attached to אמא means from. Connect it to the nominal sentence frame you already know.

The vowel of a prefix can vary with the word. Learn מֵאִמָּא as the model here; do not insist on one prefix vowel everywhere.

sourceRefs.adaptation: And is excerpted from the later source lesson; examples use the revised earlier vocabulary. Prefix vowels are word-specific models.

pages.title: Join two familiar things
pages.html:
מים ותהwater and tea

המים והתה מאמא.The water and the tea are from Mom.

ו־ means and when attached this way. It can appear before the definite prefix: והתה.

היוםtoday; also “the day” in the appropriate context

Keep the useful today meaning distinct from simply recognising the attached definite article.

pages.title: Three new anchors
pages.html:
לLamed, /l/: Guy’s source mnemonic is a ladle.

שShin, usually /sh/: the source image is a ship.

זZayin, /z/: the source image is Zorro’s sword.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The original GLD and SHZTZR groups are split to match Spiral A. Only ל/ש/ז are taught here.

pages.title: Which side has the dot?
pages.html:
שׁA dot on the right marks /sh/.

שׂA dot on the left marks /s/.

The base letter shape stays the same. The supplied words tell you which reading to use when the dots are absent.

שָׁלוֹםhello; peace

שְׂמֹאלleft — keep this whole-word reading.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The original GLD and SHZTZR groups are split to match Spiral A. Only ל/ש/ז are taught here.

pages.title: Time words in a known frame
pages.html:
לילהnight

שנהyear

הלילהtonight / the night, according to context

השנהthis year / the year, according to context

These time uses are explicit vocabulary meanings. They build on recognising ה־; the prefix alone does not supply every idiomatic time translation.

האימון הלילה.The practice/training is tonight.

lessons.prerequisites: VAV — ו sound roles; VOWELS-AEI — a/e/i and silent sheva; LSHZ — לשז.

sources.adaptation: Avoids implying that pointed and ordinary spelling are always interchangeable. Silent sheva is retrieved rather than first introduced here.

pages.title: The same vowel can have another written model
pages.html:
מֹAn /o/ mark can appear without a written Vav.

מֻThree diagonal dots supply /u/.

Connect these sounds to וֹ and וּ, which you already know. The word’s supplied spelling tells you which written form to use.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Avoids implying that pointed and ordinary spelling are always interchangeable. Silent sheva is retrieved rather than first introduced here.

pages.title: Notice the word, not just one letter
pages.html:
לֹאno / not

In this very common word, /o/ is written without Vav. In other words, a Vav may help write that vowel.

Ordinary unpointed spelling is learned with the word. Do not delete or add vowel letters mechanically whenever Nikkud appears or disappears.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Avoids implying that pointed and ordinary spelling are always interchangeable. Silent sheva is retrieved rather than first introduced here.

pages.title: Make a familiar sentence negative
pages.html:
אני אמן.I am an artist — a male speaker.

אני לא אמן.I am not an artist.

Place לא before the noun description in this familiar frame. Negative existence with אין is a later, separate connection.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Avoids implying that pointed and ordinary spelling are always interchangeable. Silent sheva is retrieved rather than first introduced here.

lessons.title: Point to one thing: זה / זאת
lessons.anchor: Use the nominal sentence frame while introducing noun gender.
lessons.prerequisites: LSHZ — לשז; NOMINAL — nominal statements; gender recognition from known nouns is introduced here.

sources.adaptation: זאת is the current early form; the source also teaches זו. Near/far claims are narrowed to these usable examples. Plural אלה remains at lesson 20.

pages.title: This is …
pages.html:
זה אמן.This is an artist — a man in this example.

זאת אמא.This is a mother.

זה and זאת point to one thing or person. The choice connects to the noun’s grammatical gender.

sourceRefs.adaptation: זאת is the current early form; the source also teaches זו. Near/far claims are narrowed to these usable examples. Plural אלה remains at lesson 20.

pages.title: Objects have grammatical gender too
pages.html:
זה יין.This is wine.

זאת מונית.This is a taxi.

Grammatical gender belongs to the noun; it does not mean an object has a biological sex. Keep the gender with the vocabulary model.

זה תות וזאת תאנה.This is a strawberry and this is a fig.

sourceRefs.adaptation: זאת is the current early form; the source also teaches זו. Near/far claims are narrowed to these usable examples. Plural אלה remains at lesson 20.

pages.title: One step at a time
pages.html:
These are complete “this is …” sentences. A phrase such as “this taxi” has a different structure, which returns after noun–adjective phrases.

For now, point, choose זה or זאת, and name one familiar thing. The plural pointing word arrives with noun plurals.

pages.title: A dot changes Bet’s sound
pages.html:
בּ/b/ with the dot in the supplied pointed model.

ב/v/ without that dot in the supplied pointed model.

Printed everyday words often omit the dots. Use the known word and its audio model; absence of all Nikkud does not itself prove a /v/ reading.

pages.title: A familiar meaning, a different form
pages.html:
ילד / ילדהboy / girl

תלמיד / תלמידהmale student / female student

דוד / דודהuncle / aunt

The feminine ending ה connects these pairs. Start with the actual paired words rather than adding an ending to every noun you see.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Uses the planned noun pairs; adjective and verb agreement remain later. Endings are clues, not an exception-free rule.

pages.title: Some pairs change more
pages.html:
איש / אישהman / woman

בן / בתson / daughter

יהודי / יהודייהJewish man / Jewish woman; masculine/feminine adjective forms

These are supplied word forms. Gender endings help, but they do not predict every pair or every object noun’s gender.

lessons.title: In, to and belonging to
lessons.anchor: Attach meanings to familiar people and places.
lessons.prerequisites: BGD בגד; PREFIXES-MHV מ,ה,ו

sources.adaptation: The relative prefix ש־ from the same source is deferred. Current examples use known words. Earlier אבל is a selected usefulness adaptation.

pages.title: In a place
pages.html:
הדג בגן.The fish is in a garden / in the garden, depending on the supplied reading and context.

ב־ attaches to the place. Pointed בְּגַן and בַּגַּן distinguish in a garden from in the garden. In ordinary unpointed print both appear as בגן.

Learn the supplied reading and meaning; do not grade this distinction from unpointed spelling alone.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The relative prefix ש־ from the same source is deferred. Current examples use known words. Earlier אבל is a selected usefulness adaptation.

pages.title: To someone; belonging to someone
pages.html:
לאמאto Mom / for Mom

המתנה של אמא.The gift belongs to Mom; in context, Mom’s gift.

ל־ attaches. של is a separate word linking a possession to its owner.

הבגד של התלמידthe student’s garment — a noun phrase

A phrase can name something without making a complete statement; context and the sentence around it matter.

sourceRefs.adaptation: The relative prefix ש־ from the same source is deferred. Current examples use known words. Earlier אבל is a selected usefulness adaptation.

pages.title: Connect two familiar statements

sourceRefs.adaptation: The relative prefix ש־ from the same source is deferred. Current examples use known words. Earlier אבל is a selected usefulness adaptation.

lessons.title: Letters כ פ צ
lessons.anchor: Return to Bet’s paired sounds and to final letters.
lessons.prerequisites: BGD — בגד; PREFIXES-BL-SHEL — ב/ל/של; earlier vowel and nominal-sentence work.

sources.adaptation: Original groups are split. Only Kaf, Pe and Tsadi are new. The linking היא example is explained before use.

pages.title: Two sound pairs
pages.html:
כּ / כ/k/ and /kh/ in the supplied pointed models; the source image is a cup/backwards C.

פּ / פ/p/ and /f/; the source image is a punch/fist.

The dot is called a dagesh. Connect the contrast to בּ / ב. In unpointed text, recover the known word rather than treating every missing dot as a soft sound.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Original groups are split. Only Kaf, Pe and Tsadi are new. The linking היא example is explained before use.

pages.title: Tsadi and final shapes
pages.html:
צ/ts/, as in the source pizza association

כ → ךKaf has a final form.

פ → ףPe has a final form.

צ → ץTsadi has a final form.

With Mem and Nun, these complete the five letters that have final shapes. A final shape does not by itself specify a hard/soft pronunciation.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Original groups are split. Only Kaf, Pe and Tsadi are new. The linking היא example is explained before use.

pages.title: Make the ownership statement explicit
pages.html:

Here היא acts as a linking pronoun. It makes the statement explicit. The shorter הכפית של אמא can also be Mom’s teaspoon as a noun phrase; it can be a statement in a suitable context.

המיץ מאבא.The juice is from Dad.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Original groups are split. Only Kaf, Pe and Tsadi are new. The linking היא example is explained before use.

pages.explanation: פ becomes ף at the end. כ becomes ך, and צ becomes ץ.

pages.title: Ask by changing the voice or punctuation
pages.html:
אתה אמן.You are an artist.

אתה אמן?Are you an artist?

The word order can stay the same. Speech uses question intonation; writing can use a question mark. האם can introduce a yes/no question in more explicit or formal phrasing.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Late source past-tense examples are omitted. Current question vocabulary and the bounded אלא contrast are supplied.

pages.title: Replace the missing information

מי זאת?Who is this?

מה זה?What is this?

איפה המפה?Where is the map?

מתי התשלום?When is the payment?

למה asks why; לאן asks where to, a destination. פה means here.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Late source past-tense examples are omitted. Current question vocabulary and the bounded אלא contrast are supplied.

זה לא תה אלא יין.This is not tea but wine.

אלא replaces a rejected identification after not. אבל links a contrast between statements.

lessons.title: There is; someone has
lessons.anchor: Combine existence with the ל־ connection you know.
lessons.prerequisites: PREFIXES-BL-SHEL — ל־ and location/possession phrases; QUESTIONS-BASIC — familiar questions; NOMINAL — nominal statements.

sources.adaptation: Source basis: current approved planning scope and examples, not a recovered video transcript. The explanation and checks are adapted draft wording.

pages.title: Say that something is there
pages.html:
יש מים.There is water.

אין מים.There is no water.

יש and אין establish existence or absence. Keep this contrast separate from לא in a sentence such as “I am not an artist”.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Source basis: current approved planning scope and examples, not a recovered video transcript. The explanation and checks are adapted draft wording.

pages.title: Connect the thing to a person
pages.html:
יש לאמא שמלה.Mom has a dress.

The useful pattern is יש + ל־ + person + thing. The person connected by ל־ is the one who has it.

למי יש מילון?Who has a dictionary?

The question builds on מי and the same ל־ connection.

sourceRefs.adaptation: Source basis: current approved planning scope and examples, not a recovered video transcript. The explanation and checks are adapted draft wording.

pages.title: Use a complete scene
pages.html:
אין מים בדלי.There is no water in the bucket.

יש מלון ליד הים.There is a hotel near the sea.

היא לבד בבית.She is alone at home.

לבד is one of the new everyday meanings. It uses the nominal frame you already know.

pages.title: A familiar noun, more than one
pages.html:
ילד → ילדיםboy / child → boys / children

ילדה → ילדותgirl → girls

תלמיד → תלמידיםmale student → male/mixed students

תלמידה → תלמידותfemale student → female students

־ים and ־ות are common plural endings. Learn the plural with the noun; the ending alone is not a universal gender test.

pages.title: Keep irregular plurals as pairs

אישה → נשיםwoman → women

בית → בתיםhouse → houses

כלב → כלביםdog → dogs

Use the supplied whole-word models. Do not generate an unlearned form merely by attaching an ending.

pages.title: Point to more than one

זאת ילדה.This is a girl.

אלה ילדות.These are girls.

אלה is the plural demonstrative here for either gender. The later demonstrative-phrase lesson returns to “these children” inside a longer noun phrase.
